transcript.speech: If you've ever tried to cancel a subscription and you think, why is this so hard?
There's a name for this. It's called the Roach Motel. This is Part 1 of my Dark Side of UX series,
not to be confused with my Build for Good UX series.
Because here I show the psychological tricks that are being played on you as a user.
On the internet, a Roach Motel is any trial or subscription that is very easy to get in, but extremely difficult to get out of.

In some cases, like LA Fitness, you might not even be able to cancel online. You have to download it, print it, mail it, or even hand-deliver it, ironically to the gym that you're canceling because you probably never go.
And you might be wondering, how's this even legal?
You have probably been through a cancellation that is so painful that you start to second-guess whether you even want to cancel anymore.
And that's literally the goal. The design is using a whole bunch of techniques just to try to get you to give up.
In 2024, the FTC passed a rule called Click to Cancel. And the rule was that canceling has to be as easy as signing up.
One-click sign-up, and then one-click cancel.
And then this rule got canceled a couple days before it was going to take effect.
So then California decided to pass something individually that went into effect July 2025, shortly followed by New York.
But these laws only apply to the customers in those states.
So technically a company could show someone in California a different cancellation flow than everybody else, even if that company itself is based in California.
And companies do get caught. Last year, Amazon paid 2.5 billion just to settle with the FTC...
...after they said canceling Prime took like 4 pages, 6 clicks, and 15 different options.
And internally, Amazon engineers literally had a name for this cancellation process: The Iliad, as in the war that lasted like 10 years.
But what are the actual psychological tricks inside of these cancellation flows?
They're called Dark Patterns, and in the next part I'm going to show you exactly how these kinds of techniques are used to keep you subscribed.

visual_demonstrations.observation: Animated mobile app screen mockup depicting multi-step cancellation friction dialogs.
visual_demonstrations.before: Screen showing initial modal titled 'Are you sure?' with a prominent button 'Keep My Plan' and a small text link 'Continue to Cancel'.
visual_demonstrations.after: Screen transitions to 'Pause instead?' modal with primary button 'Pause My Account', then to 'Confirm one more time' modal with primary button 'STAY WITH US'.

visual_demonstrations.observation: Animated UI comparison showing simple subscription and single-click cancellation.
visual_demonstrations.before: Mobile screen with 'Sign Up Now' button.
visual_demonstrations.after: Cursor clicks 'Sign Up Now', leading to subscription view where clicking 'Yes, Cancel' immediately cancels the plan.

visual_demonstrations.observation: Side-by-side / sequential UI comparison of state-specific cancellation flows (California vs Everyone else).
visual_demonstrations.before: California UI shows 'Your Subscription' with a single red 'Cancel Subscription' button that immediately shows a green checkmark 'Cancelled' screen.
visual_demonstrations.after: Everyone else UI displays a multi-step sequence: step 1 survey ('Why are you leaving?'), step 2 loss aversion warning ('You'll lose everything!'), and step 3 double confirmation screen ('Final Confirmation').

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: The 'Roach Motel' is a dark pattern where joining a subscription is effortless, but leaving is intentionally made difficult through psychological tricks and multi-step friction to force users to give up.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: UI mockups showing 3+ modal barriers ('Are you sure?', 'Pause instead?', 'Confirm one more time') contrasting with simple single-click cancellation.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Deceptive UX dark patterns that introduce artificial friction, confusing choices, and multi-step modal traps during account cancellation.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Make subscription cancellation as simple and direct as signing up ('Click to Cancel' standard).
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Provide a direct, single-click cancellation option without forcing users through surveys, loss-aversion popups, pause offers, or offline physical mail/in-person requirements.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Multi-step cancellation flows exploit psychological friction to make users second-guess or give up on canceling, leading to user frustration, regulatory scrutiny, and legal penalties.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Digital subscription products, SaaS applications, recurring billing services, and membership platforms.

analyst_interpretation.interpretation: The video highlights the legal tension and ethical considerations surrounding 'Roach Motel' dark patterns in subscription design, emphasizing regulatory efforts (like FTC Click-to-Cancel rules and California/NY legislation) aimed at requiring symmetric ease for sign-up and cancellation flows.
inferences_not_shown_or_said: The specific court rulings invalidating federal rules are referenced verbally and visually via headlines, but full judicial context is omitted.

BBC article overlay displayed: 'Amazon agrees to pay $2.5bn over claims it tricked Prime customers'.
Historical painting of Trojan War artwork with graphic text label 'the Iliad'.
